description: How firms work out costs, revenue and profit, and why profit is the central goal and signal for producers.
content_html:
Why Do Costs and Revenue Matter to a Business?

Every business needs to understand where its money comes from and where it goes. Revenue is the money flowing in; costs are the money flowing out. The difference between the two is what makes a business viable — or not. A smartphone manufacturer selling millions of handsets still goes bust if its costs are higher than its revenue. Getting this balance right is the fundamental challenge every producer faces.

Types of Cost

Costs are split into two categories based on how they behave as output changes. Fixed costs stay the same regardless of how much a firm produces. A coffee shop pays the same rent whether it serves 50 customers or 500 in a day. Fixed costs must be paid even when output is zero — which is why they are sometimes called “overhead costs.”

Variable costs, by contrast, rise and fall with output. The more coffee the shop makes, the more coffee beans, milk and cups it needs. If output doubles, variable costs roughly double too. Adding fixed and variable costs together gives total cost.

Key Fact

Total Cost = Fixed Costs + Variable Costs. Fixed costs do not change with output (e.g. rent). Variable costs rise and fall with output (e.g. raw materials).

Average cost (also called unit cost) is total cost divided by the number of units produced. If a trainers brand spends £600,000 making 20,000 pairs of shoes, the average cost is £30 per pair. Average cost matters because it determines the minimum price the firm must charge to avoid a loss. As output rises and fixed costs are spread across more units, average cost typically falls — this is the foundation of economies of scale, covered in the next lesson.

Revenue: Total and Average

Revenue is calculated by multiplying the price charged by the quantity sold. If a streaming service charges £10 per month and has 2 million subscribers, total revenue is £20 million. This is total revenue. Dividing total revenue by the number of units sold gives average revenue, which equals the price per unit in a straightforward market. Firms track total revenue closely because it determines how much money is available to cover costs.

Profit: the Central Goal

When total revenue exceeds total cost, a firm makes a profit. The formula is straightforward: Profit = Total Revenue − Total Cost. If a firm’s revenue is £500,000 and its total costs are £380,000, profit is £120,000. When total cost exceeds total revenue, the firm makes a loss.

Most private-sector businesses list profit maximisation as a primary objective. A higher profit rewards the entrepreneur for the risk they have taken and provides funds for reinvestment — new machinery, more staff, entering new markets. Without profit, a firm cannot grow or even survive in the long run.

Key Fact

Profit = Total Revenue − Total Cost. A firm increases profit by raising revenue, cutting costs, or both. Total Revenue = Price × Quantity Sold.

Profit as an Incentive and a Signal

Profit plays two roles in a market economy. First, it is an incentive: the prospect of profit motivates entrepreneurs to set up businesses, take risks and innovate. Without the reward of profit, fewer people would be willing to invest their savings or time into a new venture.

Second, profit acts as a signal. When profits are high in an industry — say, electric vehicle charging networks — this signals to other firms that there is money to be made there. New producers enter the market, increasing supply. This process steers resources to where they are most valued by consumers. Conversely, persistent losses signal that resources should move out of an industry and into more productive uses.

Profit maximisation is the dominant objective for most private firms, but it is not the only one. Some businesses prioritise sales growth — they accept lower margins to win a bigger share of the market, betting that volume will eventually deliver higher total profits. Others focus on increasing market share, which gives them greater pricing power over rivals. A new firm entering a competitive market may set prices deliberately low to attract customers and build market share — a strategy called penetration pricing. By contrast, predatory pricing is a strategy used by an existing dominant firm, which sets prices below cost specifically to drive rivals or new entrants out of the market; it is illegal under UK competition law.

There are also ethical and moral conflicts. A firm might earn higher profits by paying suppliers in lower-income countries as little as possible, or by polluting a river to avoid the cost of treating its waste water. These choices boost profit in the short run but impose costs on others — the suppliers, local communities, or the environment. This tension between private profit and wider social costs is a key theme in economics and underpins much of the debate around market failure and government intervention.

How Firms Aim to Increase Profit

There are two routes to higher profit. A firm can raise revenue — by selling more units, raising prices (if demand will bear it), or launching new products. Alternatively, it can reduce costs — by switching to cheaper suppliers, automating tasks to cut labour costs, or producing on a larger scale so that fixed costs are spread more thinly. In practice, successful firms pursue both strategies at once. A supermarket running a promotional price cut may accept lower revenue per item, gambling that the extra volume sold will lift total revenue high enough to more than compensate.

The relationship between price and revenue is not always simple. If a firm raises its price, each unit sold earns more — but if demand falls sharply as a result, total revenue may actually drop. This is why understanding price elasticity of demand (covered in the earlier unit on prices) matters so much when firms set their pricing strategy.

Students often confuse these two. The test is simple: ask “does this cost change if the firm produces one more unit?” If the answer is yes, it is a variable cost. If the answer is no, it is a fixed cost. Wages can fall into either category: a worker paid a monthly salary is a fixed cost (the bill is the same whether output is high or low), while a worker paid by the piece is a variable cost (more output means higher wages). Similarly, electricity has a standing charge (fixed) and a usage charge (variable).
exam_tip_html: For “Calculate” questions, always show your working: write the formula, substitute the numbers, then state the answer with the correct unit (usually £). For example: Profit = Total Revenue − Total Cost = £500,000 − £380,000 = £120,000. For “Explain” questions on profit, build a chain of reasoning — higher revenue and lower costs lead to higher profit — this gives the firm more funds to invest, which improves long-run competitiveness. In evaluation questions, consider whether profit maximisation conflicts with ethical responsibilities: a firm that cuts costs by exploiting workers may boost short-run profit but damage its reputation and long-run sales.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Costs are split into fixed costs (unchanged with output, e.g. rent) and variable costs (rise with output, e.g. raw materials); Total Cost = Fixed Costs + Variable Costs.
  • Total Revenue = Price × Quantity Sold; Profit = Total Revenue − Total Cost. A firm increases profit by raising revenue, cutting costs, or both.
  • Profit is both an incentive for entrepreneurs and a signal that guides resources towards where consumers value them most — but firms may face ethical conflicts between maximising profit and acting responsibly.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a fixed cost for a bakery?
A) The cost of flour used each day
B) The monthly rent on the shop premises
C) The packaging used for each loaf
D) The wages paid to part-time staff per loaf baked
practice_questions.marks: B) The monthly rent on the shop premises [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A firm produces 4,000 units in a month. Its total fixed costs are £12,000 and its variable costs are £3 per unit.
(a) Calculate the firm's total cost for the month.
(b) If the firm sells all 4,000 units at £8 each, calculate its profit.
practice_questions.marks: Part (a): 1 mark for the correct method: Total Cost = Fixed Costs + Variable Costs = £12,000 + (4,000 × £3) = £24,000; 1 mark for the correct answer of £24,000. Part (b): 1 mark for the correct method: Profit = Total Revenue − Total Cost = (4,000 × £8) − £24,000 = £32,000 − £24,000; 1 mark for the correct answer of £8,000.

practice_questions.text: Explain why profit acts as a signal in a market economy.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that high profits in an industry signal that there is money to be made there; 1 mark for developing this (e.g. new firms are attracted into the market, increasing supply); 1 mark for explaining the outcome (e.g. resources are steered towards producing goods and services that consumers value most, improving the allocation of resources in the economy).

practice_questions.text: A clothing firm is deciding whether to raise the price of its bestselling jacket from £60 to £75. Explain how this decision might affect the firm's total revenue and profit.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that total revenue = price × quantity; 1 mark for noting that the higher price increases revenue per unit sold; 1 mark for recognising that if demand falls significantly as a result of the price rise, total revenue could fall rather than rise (linking to price elasticity of demand); 1 mark for applying this to profit — if total revenue falls and costs remain the same, profit would fall, so the impact on profit depends on whether the extra revenue per unit is offset by lost sales volume.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a manufacturer of electric vehicles could increase its profits by reducing its average costs as output grows.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A sustained chain of reasoning linking rising output to falling average costs, with a developed explanation of why this raises profit margin per unit and/or makes the firm more competitive on price. May refer to the spreading of fixed costs over more units, or more efficient use of labour and machinery at scale. Concludes with a clear statement of the profit impact.
Secure (3–4 marks): A clear explanation that rising output reduces average cost, with some development of how this links to profit. May lack full development of the mechanism or the competitive implications.
Developing (2 marks): Some relevant points about costs and output, but the chain of reasoning is incomplete or the link to profit is asserted rather than explained.
Emerging (1 mark): A simple relevant point, e.g. states that higher output reduces average costs or that lower costs can increase profit.

practice_questions.text:
'Profit maximisation should always be the main objective of a private-sector business.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Profit provides the financial resources for reinvestment — new machinery, research and development, expansion into new markets — which strengthens the firm's long-run competitive position.
- Without profit, the business cannot survive; losses lead to closure, unemployment and wasted resources.
- Profit rewards the entrepreneur for taking risk and motivates innovation that benefits consumers.
- High profits signal to other producers where resources are most valued, improving overall resource allocation.

Arguments against:
- Profit maximisation can conflict with ethical responsibilities — firms may cut costs by paying poverty wages, using environmentally harmful production methods or cutting corners on quality.
- Some businesses prioritise sales growth or market share as their primary objective, accepting lower short-run profits to build long-run dominance.
- Social enterprises and cooperatives exist specifically to serve a community or social purpose, not to maximise returns to shareholders.
- Excessive focus on short-run profit can damage the firm's reputation and long-run profitability if consumers or regulators respond negatively.

Judgement (must be supported):
Mastering (8–9 marks): A balanced evaluation of both sides with a clear, supported judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. profit maximisation is appropriate for most firms in competitive markets, but it depends on the type of business, the time horizon, and whether the market is regulated — a pharmaceutical company with pricing power may need ethical constraints that a small bakery does not).
Secure (5–7 marks): Clear arguments on both sides, with an attempt at a judgement, though the judgement may lack full support.
Developing (3–4 marks): Some relevant arguments on one or both sides, but analysis is limited and judgement is absent or unsupported.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Simple relevant points with little or no development.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes a variable cost?
options: A cost that stays the same regardless of how much is produced
A cost that rises and falls directly with the level of output
The total amount a firm spends on rent and insurance
The price the firm charges per unit sold

knowledge_checks.q: A firm sells 5,000 units at £12 each. What is its total revenue?
Fixed costs do not change with the level of _____, so they must be paid even when a firm produces nothing.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: Does not change as output changes, e.g. rent
Rises and falls with output, e.g. raw materials

flashcard_questions.q: What is the formula for total cost?
flashcard_questions.a: Total Cost = Fixed Costs + Variable Costs.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a fixed cost for a restaurant.
Give one example of a variable cost for a restaurant.
What is the formula for total revenue?
What is the formula for profit?
Calculate the profit for a firm with total revenue of £900,000 and total costs of £750,000.

flashcard_questions.a: Total cost divided by the number of units produced.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does average cost typically fall as output rises?
flashcard_questions.a: Fixed costs are spread over more units, reducing the cost per unit.

flashcard_questions.q: Profit acts as a signal — what does high profit in an industry signal to other firms?
flashcard_questions.a: That there is money to be made, attracting new producers into the market.

flashcard_questions.q: Besides profit maximisation, name one other business objective.
A worker paid a fixed monthly salary is which type of cost — fixed or variable?
How can a firm raise its profit without changing its prices?
flashcard_questions.a: By reducing its costs — e.g. finding cheaper suppliers or automating production.

flashcard_questions.q: What ethical conflict can arise when a firm tries to maximise profit by cutting costs?
flashcard_questions.a: It may exploit workers or cause environmental damage to reduce expenses.

glossary_terms.definition: The total income a firm receives from selling its goods or services over a period of time.
The total expenditure a firm incurs in producing its goods or services.
Costs that do not change with the level of output, such as rent, insurance and loan repayments.
Costs that change directly with the level of output, such as raw materials, packaging and piece-rate wages.
Fixed costs plus variable costs; the total expenditure a firm incurs at any given level of output.
The total income a firm earns from selling its output, calculated as price multiplied by quantity sold.
The surplus left after total costs are subtracted from total revenue; the financial reward for the risk taken by the entrepreneur.
